questions.q: A service's unit tests use a fake repository and all pass. In production the "overdue tasks" list is always empty. What is the most likely reason the tests did not catch it?
questions.explain: A unit test is only as true as its doubles. The service logic was right; the real repository broke the promise the fake kept. Only a test of the repository against a real database, or a contract test run against both, can catch that.
options: The unit tests ran too fast to see the bug
The fake returns objects the service expects, while the real repository returns something different, such as an unmapped due_at column
Unit tests cannot test filters
The test clock was set to the wrong year

questions.q: The real repository forgot to map a column. What does this print?
questions.explain: Two days of 86,400,000 ms each land on 3 October. In a comparison, undefined becomes NaN, so every comparison is false, while null becomes 0, which is smaller than any date after 1970. Either way, a missing field silently gives a wrong answer instead of an error, which is why the mapping needs its own test.

questions.q: Which test catches a typo in the WHERE clause of PgTaskRepository.listVisibleTo most cheaply?
questions.explain: The SQL only runs in the repository against a real database. Service and CQRS tests use the fake, so they never run it. The end-to-end test may catch it, but slower, and without pointing at the line that broke.
options: A service unit test with the fake repository
A repository integration test against PGlite
The end-to-end workflow test
A CQRS test with the fake repository

questions.q: Why run one repository test suite, the contract, against both the in-memory fake and the PostgreSQL repository?
questions.explain: Service tests are only valid if the fake keeps the same promises as the real repository: duplicate titles refused, the same sort order, the same "not found". The contract checks exactly those promises for both implementations.
options: To make the suite twice as long
Because the fake needs a database
So the fake is proven to behave like the real repository, which makes the service tests that use it trustworthy
Because Vitest requires every test to run twice

questions.q: A tiny contract check runs against a fake and a real repository. What does it print?
questions.explain: The fake sorts by due date, so "Fix bike" (4 October) comes first. The "real" one returns rows in storage order. The same check fails for one implementation only, which is exactly the signal a contract test gives you.
options:
✓ fake: Fix bike
× real: Buy milk

✓ fake: Fix bike
✓ real: Fix bike

× fake: Buy milk
✓ real: Fix bike

✓ fake: Buy milk
× real: Buy milk

questions.q: Each repository test runs inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK. The test "refuses the same title twice, but allows it for another owner" fails for PostgreSQL with "current transaction is aborted". Why?
questions.explain: A failed statement breaks the whole PostgreSQL transaction. In production the second insert would not be in the same transaction and would work. The test setup changed the behaviour under test, so the lesson resets the table with TRUNCATE … RESTART IDENTITY instead.
options: PGlite does not support transactions
The unique constraint is wrong
After the duplicate insert fails inside the transaction, PostgreSQL refuses every later statement until the rollback, so the insert for the other owner is refused too
Vitest runs the two inserts in parallel

questions.q: What does TRUNCATE tasks RESTART IDENTITY before each test give you?
questions.explain: TRUNCATE removes every row, and RESTART IDENTITY resets the SERIAL sequence. It is far cheaper than starting PostgreSQL again, and unlike a wrapping transaction it does not change how errors behave during the test.
options: A new database for every test
An empty table whose id counter starts at 1 again, in about a millisecond
A rollback of the test's changes after it ends
A copy of the schema without constraints

questions.q: Why does the repository file also test that PostgreSQL refuses status = 'shipped' with code 23514?
questions.explain: Constraints are part of the schema, and schemas drift: someone edits a migration and drops the check. The fake cannot enforce it at all. A direct insert that must fail is the cheapest proof that the rule is still there.
options: Because the service cannot be trusted
The CHECK constraint is a rule only the database enforces; a test proves the migration really contains it
To test that PGlite is installed
Because TypeScript cannot check strings

questions.q: Two tests share one array. What does this print?
questions.explain: The first test leaves "Buy milk" behind, so the second one fails. Run them in the other order and both pass: a classic order-dependent, flaky suite. That is why the harness builds fresh state in beforeEach.
options:
✓ creates a task
× starts empty

✓ creates a task
✓ starts empty

× creates a task
✓ starts empty

× creates a task
× starts empty

questions.q: createAuthService has no option for a test clock. How does the lesson test that a session ends after 30 idle minutes without waiting 30 minutes?
questions.explain: Vitest can replace the global Date. toFake: ["Date"] leaves real timers alone, so other code keeps working. createTestClock only helps code that accepts a now function; it does not change the global time. Editing a token would only test the signature check.
options: It sets sessionTtlSeconds to 1 and sleeps
vi.useFakeTimers({ toFake: ["Date"] }) and vi.setSystemTime(…) move the global Date, which the auth service reads
It uses createTestClock, which changes the system time
It edits the token's exp claim

questions.q: Why does the auth test file call vi.useRealTimers() in afterEach rather than at the end of the one test that fakes time?
questions.explain: A failing assertion stops the test at that line. Cleanup written at the end of the test would never run, and every following test would see a frozen clock. Hooks are the reliable place for cleanup.
options: Because afterEach runs faster
Because afterEach runs even when the test fails halfway, so a failure cannot leave fake time behind for the next test
Because fake timers can only be undone in hooks
It makes no difference

questions.q: This session store takes its clock as a function. What does it print?
questions.explain: After 29 minutes the session is still active; after 31 it is not. Because the clock is injected, the test moves time with one assignment. No global Date is faked, and nothing else in the program is affected.
options: true false
true true
false false
false true

questions.q: Which of these belongs in your auth tests, rather than in the tests of @zudojs/auth itself?
questions.explain: Test your decisions and your wiring: the session lengths you chose, that your logout route really calls logout, that your login does not reveal which emails exist. The library's internals are covered by the library's own tests.
options: That HS256 signatures are computed correctly
That base64url decoding works
That logout ends access at once, and that a wrong password and an unknown email get the same answer
That hashPassword uses a salt

questions.q: A test for "sign out everywhere" checks that Ada's two tokens are refused. Why should it also check that Bola's token still works?
questions.explain: "Nothing else changed" is part of the behaviour. Tests that only check the intended effect miss bugs whose effect is too wide.
options: Because Vitest needs at least one passing assertion
An implementation that deleted every session of every user would pass the first half; only the second half catches it
Because Bola logged in first
To test the refresh token

questions.q: Why do the queue tests create the queue with autoProcess: false and run jobs with claimNextJob and runJob?
questions.explain: "Wait 200 ms and hope the job ran" is slow when the wait is long and flaky when it is short. Running the jobs yourself makes the test deterministic: when drain returns, nothing is left to do.
options: Because an in-memory queue cannot process jobs on its own
So the test decides exactly when jobs run, instead of waiting a guessed amount of time for background timers
To make the jobs run in parallel
Because process only works in production

questions.q: The mail server always fails, and the queue allows two attempts. What does this print?
questions.explain: attempts is the total number of tries, so the processor runs twice. runJob does not throw when the processor fails; the queue records the failure, schedules the retry, and after the last attempt moves the job to the dead-letter list. The loop waits while a retry is pending, so it only ends when both attempts are done.

questions.q: The same assignment event arrives twice and adds the same job twice. What does this print?
questions.explain: The second add with the same deduplicationKey is refused with JobDuplicateError while the first job exists, so one job waits. The notifications handler catches exactly this error, because "already queued" is success, not failure.
options:
JobDuplicateError
1

JobDuplicateError
2

questions.q: Why is the e-mail retry policy (attempts, backoff) set on the queue by createApp, and not inside registerNotifications?
questions.explain: Settings that differ between production and tests belong at the composition root, where they can be passed in. Hard-coded into the handler, the real backoff would make a retry test wait seconds.
options: Because jobs cannot have options
So production can use exponential backoff starting at a second, while tests pass a 1 ms backoff and finish three attempts instantly
Because registerNotifications runs after the queue is closed
It is only a style choice with no effect on tests

questions.q: A handler throws when it sees a task id twice. What does this print?
questions.explain: The bus runs the handler and reports the failure in the publish result instead of throwing. That is why the lesson's duplicate test checks result.failed: a handler that throws on a harmless duplicate would show up there, while the caller never notices.
options: The program crashes with "duplicate job"

questions.q: Chidi sends a command whose payload claims to be Ada. What does this print?
questions.explain: The handler reads the user from the execution context, which the HTTP layer built from a verified token. The userId in the payload is ignored. A test that sends exactly such a forged command proves the rule holds at runtime, not only in the types.
options: NotFoundError 404
done
AuthorizationError 403
AuthenticationError 401

questions.q: A command handler fails with an unexpected error. What does this print?
questions.explain: errorMiddleware wraps unknown errors in a CqrsError with status 500 and expose: false. The message is kept for your logs; expose: false tells the HTTP layer to send only a generic message. The HTTP test then checks that the client really sees nothing more.
options: CqrsError 500 false
Error undefined undefined
CqrsError 500 true
InternalServerError 500 false

questions.q: The CQRS handlers are one line each and delegate to the service. What is worth testing at this layer?
questions.explain: Repeating the service rules adds nothing: the service tests own them. What this layer adds is wiring and identity, and those are exactly the things that break silently when someone adds a command or refactors a handler.
options: Nothing, because thin code cannot break
Every service rule again, through the bus
The wiring: every command has a handler, identity comes only from the context, middleware sees every command, unexpected errors are wrapped
Only that the bus is fast

questions.q: Why do the HTTP and end-to-end tests build the app with the same createApp function as production?
questions.explain: The composition root is code too, and it can be wrong: forget processEmails and no e-mail is ever sent. Only tests that go through it can notice. Everything that must differ in tests (database, mailer, clock, queue options) comes in through its parameters.
options: Because it is shorter than building the parts by hand
So the tests exercise the real wiring; a test that wires the parts itself would pass even if createApp forgot a part
Because createApp starts PostgreSQL
Because Vitest requires a composition root

questions.q: The test harness makes PostgreSQL and the password hashes once per file, but a new app for every test. Why this split?
questions.explain: Share what is slow and can be reset; rebuild what is cheap and stateful. Truncating the table resets the database, and a new app gives new sessions, new subscriptions and an empty queue.
options: Password hashes change between tests
Starting PostgreSQL and hashing are slow and hold no per-test state once the table is truncated; buses, queues and sessions are cheap and hold state that must not leak between tests
Because Vitest does not allow more than one database
So the tests can run in any order without truncating

questions.q: Bola asks to complete a task of Ada's that he cannot see. The API answers 404, not 403. Why is that the better answer?
questions.explain: The task exists, but not for Bola. Answering 404 hides even that. The service still uses 403 where the user can see the task but may not do the action, such as an assignee trying to reassign.
options: 404 is faster to compute
A 403 would confirm that the task exists; 404 tells an outsider nothing
403 is only for missing tokens
Because the task really does not exist in the database

questions.q: The HTTP test makes the database fail once with connection reset by 10.0.0.12:5432 and expects 500 { error: "Internal Server Error" }. What is the test protecting?
questions.explain: Error messages from infrastructure often contain addresses, table names or queries, which help an attacker map your system. They belong in logs. The client gets a generic answer, and this test fails the day someone "helpfully" passes the message on.
options: The database from being called twice
That internal details such as hosts, ports and SQL never reach the client, even though the error message contains them
That the database reconnects
That the request is retried

questions.q: vi.spyOn(shared.db, "query").mockRejectedValueOnce(…) is used in one HTTP test. Why does the file call vi.restoreAllMocks() in afterEach?
questions.explain: A spy replaces a method on a real object. The failure itself happens once, but the spy wrapper stays until it is restored. On a shared object, anything left behind can change the next test.
options: To delete the database
The database object is shared by every test in the file; without restoring, the spy would stay on its query method for the following tests
Because mockRejectedValueOnce never expires
To reset the token secrets

questions.q: Which bug can only the end-to-end test in the lesson catch?
questions.explain: The notifications tests register the processor themselves, so they pass. Only a test that uses the real composition root and follows the job all the way to the mailer notices that production never registered it.
options: A non-owner can assign a task
A duplicate title is allowed
createApp never calls processEmails, so queued e-mails are never sent
A wrong password reveals that the email exists

questions.q: Which of these is not a usual cause of a flaky test?
questions.explain: Flaky tests come from things that change between runs: time, timing, shared state, ports and other programs, test order. A fixed clock and a fresh app remove two of those causes.
options: Reading the real current time
Waiting a fixed number of milliseconds for background work
Rows left behind by another test
A test that uses a fixed clock and a fresh app

questions.q: The workflow test reads the task id from the POST /tasks response instead of using 1. Why?
questions.explain: The harness does reset the id counter, so 1 would work today. Reading the id from the response makes the test depend on behaviour it checks, not on a detail of the setup.
options: Ids are random in PostgreSQL
It keeps the test correct even if the setup changes, for example if another task is created first or the table is not reset
Because expectJson cannot compare numbers
Because the HTTP client renames fields

questions.q: Your CI runs the tests in parallel against one real PostgreSQL server. What must you do?
questions.explain: Parallel test files must never share tables. PGlite gives each file its own database automatically; with a shared server you create one database (or schema) per worker.
options: Nothing: TRUNCATE is safe across workers
Give each worker its own database, for example named after VITEST_POOL_ID, because one worker's TRUNCATE would delete another worker's rows mid-test
Run every test inside BEGIN and ROLLBACK
Turn off the unique constraints

questions.q: A cleanup list stops things in reverse order. What does this print?
questions.explain: Last started, first stopped: the server stops taking requests before the queue and the database it uses go away. createCleanupManager does the same, and reports every cleanup that fails.
options: start database, start queue, start http server, stop http server, stop queue, stop database
start database, start queue, start http server, stop database, stop queue, stop http server
stop http server, stop queue, stop database
start database, stop database, start queue, stop queue, start http server, stop http server

questions.q: Rows are sorted by due date with the id as a tie-breaker. What does this print?
questions.explain: Task 2 is due first. Tasks 1 and 3 share a date, so localeCompare returns 0 and || falls through to the id. Without the tie-breaker, their order would depend on storage order, which PostgreSQL changes when a row is updated.

questions.q: What does this retry helper print?
questions.explain: The first call fails once and works on the second try. The second always fails and gives up after two attempts with the last error. A "fail once, then work" double, like mockRejectedValueOnce, is how you test the first case.
options:
sent after 2
gave up: SMTP 550

sent after 1
gave up: SMTP 550

sent after 2
gave up: SMTP 421

gave up: SMTP 421
gave up: SMTP 550

questions.q: The tests create the table with the same migrate function production uses. What goes wrong with a separate, hand-written test schema?
questions.explain: The point of a repository integration test is to run against the real schema. Two copies of a schema always drift apart eventually, and the tests then prove nothing about production.
options: Nothing, as long as it has the same table name
It drifts: a constraint or column added to the real migration is missing in tests, so the tests pass against a database that does not exist anywhere
PGlite cannot run hand-written SQL
It makes the tests slower

questions.q: Write drain(queue): run jobs with claimNextJob and runJob until none is left. When no job is ready but getStats() reports retrying or delayed jobs, wait 5 ms and try again.
questions.explain: After the first failure the job is retrying and not yet claimable, so claimNextJob returns null. Returning then would end the test before the retry. Checking the stats and waiting briefly lets the retry run; the loop ends only when nothing is pending.

questions.q: Make the fake repository's create refuse a second task with the same title for the same owner (throw an Error whose message contains already have), and allow it for a different owner. The contract checks at the bottom must print three ✓ lines.
questions.explain: The real table has UNIQUE (owner_id, title), so the fake must enforce the same pair, not the title alone. A fake that refused the title for everyone would make service tests pass or fail for reasons production never has; the contract suite is what catches such a difference.
questions.expected:
✓ first task is created
✓ same title, same owner is refused
✓ same title, other owner is fine

questions.q: Write userOf(context): return context.userId, or throw an AuthenticationError from @zudojs/errors with the message Sign in first when there is no user. The handler must never read the user from the command.
questions.explain: The command's userId: "chidi" is ignored: identity comes from the context, which the HTTP layer builds from a verified token. With no user in the context the handler refuses with a 401 instead of acting for nobody.
questions.expected:
ada created Buy milk
AuthenticationError 401 Sign in first

questions.q: Write createClock(iso) for tests: now() returns a Date for the current fake time, and advance(ms) moves it forward. The service below takes now as a function.
questions.explain: The clock keeps a number and returns a new Date each time, so no caller can change the clock by mutating a date it received. createTestClock from @zudojs/testing is the full version, with add({ days }) and set(date).

questions.q: Write toTask(row), which turns a database row (owner_id, assignee_id, due_at, …) into a task object (ownerId, assigneeId, dueAt, …). The checks print what is wrong until every field is mapped.
questions.explain: This is the mapping the opening example forgot. With the raw row, task.dueAt is undefined, the comparison is false and the task is "not overdue". In TypeScript, giving toTask a Task return type makes the compiler catch a missing field; the repository contract test catches a wrong one.

questions.q: Write runContract(name, makeRepository): for each check in checks, make a fresh repository, run the check with it, and print ✓ name: check or × name: check. Run it for both repositories.
questions.explain: A fresh repository per check keeps the checks independent, just like beforeEach in the lesson's contract. The same checks, run against two implementations, show that only the "real" one breaks the sort promise.
questions.expected:
✓ fake: starts empty
✓ fake: sorts by due date
✓ real: starts empty
× real: sorts by due date

questions.q: Write failOnce(error, value): it returns an async function that rejects with error on its first call and resolves to value on every later call. It also counts its calls in fn.calls.
questions.explain: This is what vi.fn().mockRejectedValueOnce(error).mockResolvedValue(value) gives you in Vitest: a dependency that fails once, then recovers, which is the case a retry must handle.

questions.q: Sort the tasks by due, and tasks with the same due by id, without changing the original array.
questions.explain: Comparing the date first and falling back to the id with || gives a total order, so the fake and the SQL ORDER BY due_at, id agree on every list. toSorted returns a new array and leaves tasks as it was.
questions.expected:
Fix bike, Book taxi, Pack bags, Call Ada
3
